questions.q: Which of these is a reliable measure of how hot or cold a body is?
o: How it feels when we touch it
How long it was kept in the sun
How much steam rises from it
questions.a: Its temperature: temperature is a reliable measure of hotness or coldness, while our sense of touch can mislead us.

questions.q: Meera keeps her left hand in a bowl of ice-cold water for two minutes. She then takes it out and puts the same hand into a bucket of tap water. How will the tap water most likely feel to her left hand?
o: Exactly as it feels to a hand kept in the air
questions.a: Warm: a hand that has just been in ice-cold water feels tap water as warm, which shows that touch cannot always judge hotness correctly.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A cup of milk at 60 °C is hotter than a cup of milk at 45 °C.
Reason (R): A hotter body has a higher temperature than a colder body.
Choose the correct option.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A: 60 °C is the higher temperature, and a higher temperature means a hotter body.

questions.q: True or False: 'The difference between the temperatures of two bodies tells us how much hotter one body is than the other.' Give the verdict and one example with numbers.
questions.a: True. Example: water at 50 °C and water at 30 °C differ by 20 °C, so the first is 20 °C hotter than the second.
s: An example with two temperatures and their difference worked out correctly

questions.q: (a) What is temperature? (b) Name the device used to measure it.
questions.a: (a) Temperature is a reliable measure of the hotness or coldness of a body. (b) A thermometer.
s: (a) Temperature: a reliable measure of how hot or cold a body is

questions.q:
Answer each part in one line.
(a) Which sense do we use when we dip a finger in water to judge whether it is hot or cold?
(b) Can this sense always tell us correctly whether a body is hot or cold?
(c) Name the two kinds of thermometers we are most likely to come across.
questions.a: (a) The sense of touch. (b) No, we cannot always rely on touch to decide correctly whether a body is hot or cold. (c) Clinical thermometers and laboratory thermometers.
s: (b) No, touch cannot always judge it correctly

questions.q: Anu says water sample P feels hotter, but Biju says sample Q feels hotter. A thermometer reads P at 34 °C and Q at 31 °C. Which conclusion is correct?
o: They cannot be compared, as the two students felt them differently
questions.a: P is hotter, by 3 °C: the thermometer readings decide it (34 °C - 31 °C = 3 °C), whatever the two hands felt.

questions.q:
A bottle of water from the refrigerator reads 8 °C and a jug of water kept on the table reads 27 °C.
(a) Which has the higher temperature, and by how many degrees?
(b) Irfan has been holding ice cubes and says the bottle water 'does not feel cold at all'. Why should his feeling not be trusted?
questions.a: (a) The jug, by 27 °C - 8 °C = 19 °C. (b) His hand was just in something colder (ice), so cold water can feel warmer than it is; touch depends on what the hand felt before, so it cannot always judge hotness correctly.
s: (b) His hand was colder from the ice, so touch misleads; only the reading can be trusted

questions.q:
A vegetable seller in Kolkata keeps leafy vegetables fresh in three tubs of water. Tub 1 has water from the roof tank, tub 2 has water from a clay pot and tub 3 has water with ice in it. At noon a customer who is a science teacher measures them with a thermometer: tub 1 is at 36 °C, tub 2 at 26 °C and tub 3 at 9 °C. The seller, whose hands have been in tub 3 all morning, says tub 2 feels 'quite warm'. His helper, whose hands have been in tub 1, says tub 2 feels 'cold'.
(a) Arrange the tubs from the coldest to the hottest.
(b) By how many degrees is tub 1 hotter than tub 2?
(c) Why did tub 2 feel warm to the seller?
(d) Is the water in tub 2 at two different temperatures, as the two men's words suggest? Explain using the readings.
questions.a: (a) Tub 3 (9 °C), tub 2 (26 °C), tub 1 (36 °C). (b) 36 °C - 26 °C = 10 °C. (c) His hands had been in much colder water (tub 3), so water at 26 °C felt warm to them. (d) No: tub 2 has one temperature, 26 °C; the two men felt it differently only because their hands had been in water of different temperatures, which shows touch is not a reliable measure.
s: (c) His hands were in colder water before, so tub 2 felt warm
(d) No, one temperature of 26 °C; the feelings differ because of where each hand had been

questions.q:
Three beakers stand on a bench. Beaker P is 12 °C hotter than beaker Q, and beaker R is 5 °C colder than beaker Q. A thermometer in P reads 40 °C.
(a) Find the temperatures of Q and R.
(b) By how many degrees is P hotter than R?
(c) After keeping her hand in P, Mona dips it in R and says, 'R is almost as cold as ice water.' Check her claim.
questions.a: (a) Q = 40 °C - 12 °C = 28 °C; R = 28 °C - 5 °C = 23 °C. (b) 40 °C - 23 °C = 17 °C. (c) Her claim is not right: R is at 23 °C, far from ice-cold; it felt very cold only because her hand had just been in P, which is 17 °C hotter, and touch cannot always judge hotness correctly.
s: (c) Claim wrong: R is 23 °C; it felt cold because her hand came from hotter water

questions.q: A doctor tells Riya that her thermometer reading is exactly the value taken as the normal temperature of a healthy human body. What did the thermometer show?
questions.a: 37.0 °C: the normal temperature of a healthy human body is taken to be 37.0 °C (98.6 is the same temperature on the Fahrenheit scale, not in °C).

questions.q: Kabir wants to measure his temperature with a digital clinical thermometer after washing his hands and its tip. In which order should he do the next steps?
o: Press reset, place it under the tongue and close the mouth, wait for the beep or flash, then take it out and read
Place it under the tongue and close the mouth, read the display at once without waiting, then press the reset button
Press reset, hold it by the tip in the hand until it beeps or flashes, then place it under the tongue and read it
Place it under the tongue, take it out after the beep or flash, then press the reset button and read the display
questions.a: Press reset, place it under the tongue and close the mouth, wait for the beep or flash, then take it out and read the display.

questions.q:
Match each thermometer in Column I with its use in Column II.
Column I: 1. Digital clinical thermometer  2. Laboratory thermometer  3. Non-contact (infrared) thermometer  4. Room thermometer
Column II: A. Gives an approximate idea of the temperature of a room  B. Measures a person's temperature without touching the body  C. Measures human body temperature when placed in contact with the body  D. Used for many other purposes, such as the temperature of water in a beaker
questions.a: 1-C, 2-D, 3-B, 4-A: the clinical thermometer touches the body, the laboratory thermometer has many other uses, the infrared one works without touching, and the room thermometer gives an approximate room temperature.

questions.q: State two precautions to be taken while using a digital clinical thermometer.
questions.a: Any two of: read the instruction manual before use; wash the tip with soap and water before and after use; keep the digital portion such as the display out of water while washing; do not hold the thermometer by the tip.

questions.q: Right after running a 400 m race on sports day, a healthy girl's temperature is measured under the tongue and reads 37.4 °C. True or False: 'This reading alone need not mean that she has a fever.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. Body temperature is influenced by factors such as activity level, and 37.0 °C is only the average for many healthy people, so a healthy person can read slightly more than 37.0 °C.
s: Reason: activity level affects body temperature and 37.0 °C is only an average

questions.q: Ayaan, who is healthy, measures his temperature under the tongue at 6 am and again at 4 pm on the same day. The readings are 36.5 °C and 37.1 °C. Which explanation fits best?
o: Body temperature is influenced by the time of the day
The thermometer must be faulty, as the two readings differ
He has a fever at 4 pm, as the reading is above 37.0 °C
The Celsius scale itself shifts during the day
questions.a: Body temperature is influenced by the time of the day (as well as age and activity level), so small changes in a healthy person are normal.

questions.q:
Five healthy classmates measure their temperatures under the tongue: 36.7 °C, 37.2 °C, 36.9 °C, 37.3 °C and 36.9 °C.
(a) How many of them read exactly 37.0 °C?
(b) Find the average of the five readings.
(c) A sixth healthy classmate reads 36.6 °C and says she must be unwell because she is 'below normal'. Is she right? Give a reason.
questions.a: (a) None of them. (b) (36.7 + 37.2 + 36.9 + 37.3 + 36.9) / 5 = 185.0 / 5 = 37.0 °C. (c) No: 37.0 °C is the average body temperature of many healthy people, so a perfectly healthy person may read slightly different from it, as these five do.
s: (c) No, normal is an average; healthy people vary slightly around it

questions.q:
At a school health room in Raipur, the nurse checks four students with a digital clinical thermometer. Her notes read: Tanvi, under the tongue, 37.0 °C; Imran, under the tongue, 38.4 °C; Kavya, in the armpit, 36.6 °C; Jojo, under the tongue, 37.2 °C. She washes the tip with soap and water before and after each student.
(a) Whose reading is exactly the value taken as normal body temperature?
(b) Who has the highest reading?
(c) Is Kavya's actual body temperature higher or lower than 36.6 °C? By about how much?
(d) Name the scale on which these readings are given.
questions.a: (a) Tanvi (37.0 °C). (b) Imran (38.4 °C). (c) Higher: an armpit reading is about 0.5 °C to 1 °C lower than the actual body temperature. (d) The Celsius scale.

questions.q:
A family in Imphal checks their 70-year-old grandmother with a digital thermometer in the armpit each evening. The readings are: Day 1, 36.4 °C; Day 2, 37.1 °C; Day 3, 37.6 °C. Their doctor said, 'Call me if her ACTUAL body temperature reaches 38.0 °C or more.' An armpit reading is about 0.5 °C to 1 °C lower than the actual body temperature.
(a) Work out the likely range of her actual temperature on each of the three days.
(b) On which day had her actual temperature surely reached 38.0 °C?
(c) On which day can the family not be sure from the armpit reading alone?
(d) Her cousin says, 'All three readings are below 38.0 °C, so there is no need to call the doctor.' Evaluate this and say what the family should do.
questions.a: (a) Day 1: 36.9 °C to 37.4 °C; Day 2: 37.6 °C to 38.1 °C; Day 3: 38.1 °C to 38.6 °C. (b) Day 3, since even the lowest estimate (38.1 °C) is above 38.0 °C. (c) Day 2: the actual value may be 37.6 °C (below) or up to 38.1 °C (above). (d) The cousin is wrong: he compared armpit readings with a rule about actual body temperature without adding 0.5 °C to 1 °C. On Day 3 her actual temperature was surely 38.0 °C or more, so the family should call the doctor.
s: (a) Day 1 and Day 2 ranges correct (36.9-37.4 °C and 37.6-38.1 °C)
(d) Cousin wrong because armpit readings run lower; call the doctor

questions.q:
Read the statements.
Statement I: A clinical thermometer is used to measure human body temperature, and a laboratory thermometer is used for many other purposes.
Statement II: A healthy person always has a body temperature of exactly 37.0 °C.
Statement III: Body temperature is influenced by factors such as age, time of the day and activity level.
Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: I and III only. Statement II is wrong: 37.0 °C is an average, and a perfectly healthy person may have a normal temperature slightly different from it.

questions.q: Which of these is the SI unit of temperature, written correctly?
questions.a: kelvin (K): the SI unit of temperature is the kelvin, and its symbol K is written without a degree sign.

questions.q: The water in a school's drinking-water cooler is at 12 °C. What is this temperature on the Kelvin scale?
questions.a: 285.15 K: temperature in kelvin = 12 + 273.15 = 285.15 K.

questions.q: (a) Name the three temperature scales described in the chapter. (b) Write the symbol of the unit used on each of them.
questions.a: (a) The Celsius scale, the Fahrenheit scale and the Kelvin scale. (b) °C (degree Celsius), °F (degree Fahrenheit) and K (kelvin).

questions.q:
Answer each part in one line.
(a) A healthy body temperature of 37.0 °C is equal to how many degrees on the Fahrenheit scale?
(b) Which of the three scales is not used in most scientific studies any more?
(c) Which scale is used in scientific work and gives the SI unit of temperature?
questions.a: (a) 98.6 °F. (b) The Fahrenheit scale. (c) The Kelvin scale (unit kelvin, K).

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Water at 20 °C is at 293.15 K.
Reason (R): To change a temperature in kelvin into degrees Celsius, we add 273.15 to it.
Choose the correct option.
o: A is true, but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: A is true, but R is false: 20 + 273.15 = 293.15 K, but to go from kelvin to degrees Celsius we subtract 273.15; we add 273.15 only when going from Celsius to kelvin.

questions.q:
Read the statements about writing and changing temperatures.
Statement I: The name of the unit kelvin starts with a lower-case letter.
Statement II: Temperature in kelvin = temperature in degrees Celsius - 273.15.
Statement III: The Fahrenheit scale is the scale used in most scientific studies today.
Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: I only. Statement II is wrong because 273.15 is added, not subtracted, to change degrees Celsius into kelvin. Statement III is wrong because the Fahrenheit scale is not used in most scientific studies any more.

questions.q: True or False: 'A beaker of water at 300 K is colder than a beaker of water at 20 °C.' Give the verdict and show your working.
questions.a: False. 300 K = 300 - 273.15 = 26.85 °C, which is higher than 20 °C, so the beaker at 300 K is the hotter one.

questions.q: For a science fair chart, a Class 6 student in Srinagar has measured four temperatures in degrees Celsius. She must write each one on the Kelvin scale. Convert each: (a) a cup of kahwa at 70 °C; (b) the classroom at 18 °C; (c) tap water at 9 °C; (d) a healthy body at its normal temperature of 37.0 °C.
questions.a: Temperature in kelvin = temperature in °C + 273.15. (a) 343.15 K (b) 291.15 K (c) 282.15 K (d) 310.15 K.

questions.q:
A pharmacy in Panaji sells two digital thermometers. On a healthy customer, one of them shows 37.0 and the other shows 98.6; neither display shows a unit. A box of syrup in the shop says: 'Store below 298.15 K.' The pharmacist has two places to keep it: a storeroom whose room thermometer reads about 296 K on a sensor that works in kelvin, and a display shelf where a room thermometer reads about 26 °C.
(a) On which scale is the thermometer that shows 98.6 reading?
(b) Write the storage limit 298.15 K in degrees Celsius.
(c) Write the storeroom's 296 K in degrees Celsius.
(d) Where should the syrup be kept? Justify with your answers to (b) and (c).
questions.a: (a) The Fahrenheit scale, since 37.0 °C is equal to 98.6 °F. (b) 298.15 - 273.15 = 25 °C. (c) 296 - 273.15 = 22.85 °C. (d) In the storeroom: 22.85 °C is below the 25 °C limit, while the display shelf at about 26 °C is above it.
s: (d) Storeroom, because 22.85 °C is below 25 °C and the shelf's 26 °C is above it

questions.q: Liquid X is at -40 °C and liquid Y is at 235 K. Which statement is correct?
o: They are equally cold, as both are below 0 °C
questions.a: X is colder, by 1.85 °C: -40 °C = -40 + 273.15 = 233.15 K, which is 235 - 233.15 = 1.85 K (the same as 1.85 °C) below Y.

questions.q: On a laboratory thermometer, the temperature reading is the mark of the Celsius scale with which ______ coincides. What fills the gap?
o: the top level of the liquid column
the middle of the liquid column
the first bigger mark above the bulb
questions.a: The top level of the liquid column: the scale mark it coincides with is the temperature reading.

questions.q: On a laboratory thermometer, two bigger marks are 20 °C apart and there are 10 small divisions between them. How much temperature does one small division show?
questions.a: 2 °C: one small division = 20 °C / 10 divisions = 2 °C.

questions.q:
Match each part or term of a laboratory thermometer in Column I with its description in Column II.
Column I: 1. Bulb  2. Liquid column  3. Range  4. Smallest division
Column II: A. The span from the lowest to the highest temperature the thermometer can measure  B. The temperature shown by one small mark-to-mark gap on the scale  C. The part at one end of the tube that contains the liquid  D. Rises or falls as the temperature changes
questions.a: 1-C, 2-D, 3-A, 4-B: the bulb holds the liquid, the liquid column rises or falls with temperature, the range is the lowest-to-highest span, and the smallest division is the value of one small gap.

questions.q: (a) What is meant by the range of a laboratory thermometer? (b) What range does a laboratory thermometer typically have?
questions.a: (a) The range is the span from the lowest temperature to the highest temperature that the thermometer can measure. (b) From -10 °C to 110 °C.
s: (a) Range: lowest to highest temperature it can measure

questions.q:
A laboratory thermometer in a school in Ranchi has its lowest mark at -10 °C and its highest mark at 110 °C. Its bigger marks are 10 °C apart, and there are 5 small divisions between any two bigger marks. Its liquid is coloured red.
(a) What is the range of this thermometer?
(b) How much temperature does one small division show?
(c) The top of the liquid column is 3 small divisions above the 30 °C mark. What is the reading?
(d) Can this thermometer measure a temperature of 125 °C? Why?
(e) Which liquid, coloured red to be seen easily, is generally used in such thermometers?
questions.a: (a) -10 °C to 110 °C. (b) 10 °C / 5 = 2 °C. (c) 30 °C + 3 x 2 °C = 36 °C. (d) No, 125 °C is above its highest mark of 110 °C, outside its range. (e) Alcohol.

questions.q: On a laboratory thermometer the bigger marks are 5 °C apart, with 10 small divisions between two bigger marks. The top of the liquid column is 3 small divisions BELOW the 25 °C mark. What is the reading?
questions.a: 23.5 °C: one small division = 5 °C / 10 = 0.5 °C, so the reading is 25 °C - 3 x 0.5 °C = 23.5 °C.

questions.q:
Nisha is designing a thermometer scale in which the bigger marks are 5 °C apart and each small division reads 0.2 °C.
(a) How many small divisions must she draw between two bigger marks?
(b) On her finished thermometer, the top of the liquid column is 8 small divisions above the 30 °C mark. What is the reading?

Thermometer M reads from -10 °C to 110 °C and has 10 small divisions between bigger marks that are 10 °C apart. Thermometer N reads from 20 °C to 50 °C and has 10 small divisions between bigger marks that are 5 °C apart.
(a) Find the smallest division of each thermometer.
(b) Which one can show a reading of 46.5 °C on a mark?
(c) Which one must be used to follow water being heated from 30 °C to 80 °C? Why?
questions.a: (a) M: 10 °C / 10 = 1 °C; N: 5 °C / 10 = 0.5 °C. (b) N, since 46.5 °C is a multiple of 0.5 °C and lies inside its range, while M reads only whole degrees. (c) M, because N's range ends at 50 °C and cannot show 80 °C, while M goes up to 110 °C.
s: (c) M, because N's range stops at 50 °C

questions.q:
A special thermometer has its lowest mark at -5 °C and its highest mark at 55 °C. Bigger marks are drawn every 5 °C (-5 °C, 0 °C, 5 °C and so on), and there are 25 small divisions between any two bigger marks.
(a) What is its range, and how many degrees does that range span?
(b) How much temperature does one small division show?
(c) How many small divisions are there in all from the lowest mark to the highest mark?
(d) The top of the liquid column is 17 small divisions above the 35 °C mark. What is the reading?
(e) Could this thermometer be used to read the temperature of water boiling in a beaker? Explain.
questions.a: (a) -5 °C to 55 °C, a span of 55 - (-5) = 60 °C. (b) 5 °C / 25 = 0.2 °C. (c) 60 °C / 0.2 °C = 300 small divisions. (d) 35 °C + 17 x 0.2 °C = 35 °C + 3.4 °C = 38.4 °C. (e) No: boiling water is far hotter than 55 °C (boiling-water readings taken in Shillong were about 98 °C), so it lies outside this thermometer's range.
s: (e) No, boiling water is far above 55 °C, outside the range

questions.q: A school lab must record the temperature of warm water that will stay between 30 °C and 60 °C, to the nearest 0.5 °C. It can buy one of three thermometers. A: range -10 °C to 110 °C, smallest division 1 °C. B: range 0 °C to 50 °C, smallest division 0.5 °C. C: range 20 °C to 80 °C, with 10 small divisions between bigger marks that are 5 °C apart. Which should it buy? Check each one and justify your choice.
questions.a: A covers 30 °C to 60 °C but reads only to 1 °C, so it cannot show half degrees. B reads to 0.5 °C but its range stops at 50 °C, so it cannot show 50 °C to 60 °C. C has smallest division 5 °C / 10 = 0.5 °C and its range of 20 °C to 80 °C covers 30 °C to 60 °C. So the lab should buy C, the only one that meets both needs.
s: Rejects A: smallest division 1 °C is too coarse
Rejects B: range ends at 50 °C, below 60 °C
Finds C's smallest division 0.5 °C and checks its range covers 30-60 °C

questions.q: While reading a laboratory thermometer standing in a beaker of warm water, where should your eye be?
o: In line with the level of the liquid column
Above the level of the column, looking down at it
Below the level of the column, looking up at it
In line with the bulb at the bottom
questions.a: Directly in line with the level of the liquid column to be read.

questions.q:
Read the statements about measuring the temperature of warm water with a laboratory thermometer.
Statement I: The thermometer should be held vertically and not tilted.
Statement II: Its bulb should not touch the bottom or the sides of the beaker.
Statement III: The temperature should be read while the thermometer is still immersed in the water.
Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: All three: hold it vertically, keep the bulb away from the bottom and sides, and read it while it is still immersed.

questions.q: True or False: 'To read a laboratory thermometer accurately, take it out of the warm water and then read it closely.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: False. As soon as the thermometer is taken out of the water, the level of the liquid column begins to fall, so it must be read while it is still immersed in the water.
s: Reason: the column starts falling once it is out, so read it while immersed

questions.q:
Jaya dips a laboratory thermometer into a beaker of warm water and watches the liquid column rise.
(a) When should she note the temperature?
(b) Why should she not wait too long after that?
questions.a: (a) When the liquid column stops rising. (b) If she waits too long, the water itself will start to cool, so the reading will no longer be the temperature she wanted.
s: (b) The water itself starts to cool if she waits too long

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The temperature of warm water must be read while the bulb of the laboratory thermometer is still in the water.
Reason (R): As soon as the thermometer is taken out of the water, the level of the liquid column begins to fall.
Choose the correct option.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A: because the column starts falling once the thermometer is out, the reading must be taken while it is immersed.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): While water is boiling, a laboratory thermometer kept in it shows the same reading again and again.
Reason (R): A laboratory thermometer should be held vertically and not tilted.
Choose the correct option.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A: the reading stays the same because the temperature of water remains constant while it is boiling; holding the thermometer upright is only a rule for reading it correctly.

(a) The clinical thermometer is placed under the tongue with the mouth closed (or in the armpit); the laboratory thermometer's bulb is immersed in the water without touching the bottom or sides of the beaker. (b) The clinical thermometer is taken out after it beeps or flashes and then read; the laboratory thermometer must be read while it is still immersed. (c) The clinical thermometer must not be held by its tip; the laboratory thermometer must not be held by its bulb.
s: (a) Under the tongue versus bulb immersed in water, clear of the beaker
(b) Clinical read after taking it out; laboratory read while still immersed
(c) Clinical not held by the tip; laboratory not held by the bulb

questions.q:
In a Class 6 science lab in Indore, four students measure the same beaker of warm water, one after another, within one minute, using the same kind of laboratory thermometer. Esha holds it vertically with the bulb clear of the beaker, keeps her eye level with the liquid column and reads it in the water: 52 °C. Farhan lifts it out of the water and reads it a few seconds later: 49 °C. Gita tilts it so that it leans on the rim of the beaker: 54 °C. Hari does exactly what Esha did: 52 °C.
(a) Which students followed the correct way?
(b) Why is Farhan's reading lower than Esha's?
(c) Name one mistake in Gita's method.
(d) The group must record one temperature. Which value should it record? Justify.
questions.a: (a) Esha and Hari. (b) Once the thermometer is out of the water, the liquid column begins to fall, so a reading taken outside the water comes out lower. (c) She tilted the thermometer; it should be held vertically. (d) 52 °C: the two students who followed every rule got the same reading, while Farhan's and Gita's readings came from wrong methods and should not be used.
s: (b) Column falls once the thermometer is out of the water
(c) Tilted the thermometer instead of holding it vertically
(d) 52 °C, the matching reading from the two correct methods

questions.q: Rohit's mother asks him to find the temperature of the warm water in a deep steel pot before she mixes it into dough. He has a laboratory thermometer. Write, in order, four things he must do from dipping the thermometer to recording the reading, and give the reason for the step about when to read it.
questions.a: 1. Dip it so the bulb is fully in the water but does not touch the bottom or sides of the pot. 2. Hold it vertically, without tilting it. 3. Wait until the liquid column stops rising, but not too long, or the water will start to cool. 4. Read it with the eye in line with the top of the liquid column while the bulb is still in the water, because the column starts to fall as soon as the thermometer is taken out.
s: Bulb immersed, not touching the bottom or sides
Waits until the column stops rising, not too long
Reads at eye level while still immersed, with the reason that the column falls once it is out

questions.q:
In a supervised activity, a teacher heats a beaker of water and a student reads a laboratory thermometer in it every 2 minutes, following the correct method: 0 min, 28 °C; 2 min, 45 °C; 4 min, 61 °C; 6 min, 76 °C; 8 min, 89 °C; 10 min, 96 °C; 12 min, 96 °C; 14 min, 96 °C. The water is boiling from the 10th minute. At 14 minutes another student reads the same thermometer and writes 93 °C.
(a) By how many degrees did the temperature rise in the first 2 minutes?
(b) In which 2-minute gap was the rise the smallest before boiling began?
(c) What happens to the temperature of the water once it is boiling? Use the data.
(d) Give one likely reason for the second student's 93 °C.
(e) What value should be recorded as the temperature of this boiling water?
questions.a: (a) 45 °C - 28 °C = 17 °C. (b) 8 to 10 minutes: 96 °C - 89 °C = 7 °C (the other gaps are 17, 16, 15 and 13 °C). (c) It stays constant at 96 °C from 10 to 14 minutes; the temperature of water remains constant while it is boiling. (d) The correct way of reading was probably not followed, for example the thermometer was read after being lifted out or the eye was not level with the column. (e) 96 °C.
s: (d) A reading mistake, such as reading it out of the water or not at eye level

questions.q: (a) Name two places where room thermometers are often hung on the walls. (b) What do room thermometers tell us?
questions.a: (a) Any two of: a school laboratory, a doctor's clinic, a hospital. (b) They give an approximate idea of the temperature of the room.
s: (b) An approximate idea of the room temperature

questions.q:
Answer each part in one line.
(a) Name two sources where we can find a weather report.
(b) Which two air temperatures of the day does a weather report mention?
(c) Generally, what happens to the air temperature as we approach the summer season?
questions.a: (a) Any two of: newspapers, TV news, the internet. (b) The maximum and the minimum air temperature of the day. (c) It generally rises.
s: (a) Two sources such as newspapers, TV news or the internet

questions.q:
Pallavi copied a weather report for Jodhpur for five days. Maximum air temperature: Monday 38 °C, Tuesday 39 °C, Wednesday 41 °C, Thursday 40 °C, Friday 42 °C. Minimum air temperature: Monday 24 °C, Tuesday 25 °C, Wednesday 26 °C, Thursday 27 °C, Friday 28 °C.
(a) On which day was the maximum air temperature the highest?
(b) What was the lowest minimum air temperature of the five days?
(c) Find the difference between the maximum and the minimum air temperature on Wednesday.
(d) Did the maximum air temperature stay at the same level on all five days?
(e) Is the air temperature generally rising or falling, and which season is most likely approaching?
questions.a: (a) Friday (42 °C). (b) 24 °C, on Monday. (c) 41 °C - 26 °C = 15 °C. (d) No, it varied from day to day (38 °C to 42 °C). (e) Generally rising, so summer is most likely approaching.

questions.q:
Class 6 students in Madurai hang a room thermometer on their classroom wall and read it three times on one day: 29 °C at 9 am, 32 °C at 12 noon and 33 °C at 3 pm. That evening, the TV weather report gives the city's maximum air temperature for the day as 36 °C and the minimum as 26 °C.
(a) At what time was the room thermometer reading the highest?
(b) By how many degrees did the room reading rise from 9 am to 3 pm?
(c) Find the difference between the day's maximum and minimum air temperature.
(d) What kind of idea of the room's temperature does a room thermometer give?
questions.a: (a) At 3 pm (33 °C). (b) 33 °C - 29 °C = 4 °C. (c) 36 °C - 26 °C = 10 °C. (d) An approximate idea of the room temperature.

questions.q: Mehul copied the maximum and minimum air temperature of the day from the newspaper for four days. Which entry must contain a copying mistake?
questions.a: Day 3: maximum 21 °C, minimum 24 °C, because the minimum air temperature of a day cannot be higher than the maximum of the same day.

questions.q:
A weather report gives these maximum and minimum air temperatures for one day: Patna 33 °C and 21 °C; Kanpur 29 °C and 24 °C; Jaipur 37 °C and 23 °C; Bikaner 34 °C and 17 °C. Match each description in Column I with the city in Column II.
Column I: 1. Highest maximum air temperature  2. Lowest minimum air temperature  3. Smallest gap between maximum and minimum  4. A gap of exactly 12 °C between maximum and minimum
Column II: A. Patna  B. Kanpur  C. Jaipur  D. Bikaner
questions.a: 1-C, 2-D, 3-B, 4-A: Jaipur has the highest maximum (37 °C), Bikaner the lowest minimum (17 °C), Kanpur the smallest gap (29 - 24 = 5 °C) and Patna a gap of 33 - 21 = 12 °C.

questions.q:
A newspaper gives Shillong's maximum and minimum air temperatures as 22 °C and 13 °C for Monday, and 24 °C and 14 °C for Tuesday.
(a) By how many degrees did the maximum air temperature change from Monday to Tuesday, and in which direction?
(b) Ama says, 'So Tuesday was warmer than Monday at every hour of the day.' Can the report tell us this? Give a reason.
questions.a: (a) It rose by 24 °C - 22 °C = 2 °C. (b) No: the report gives only the day's maximum and minimum air temperatures, not the temperature at every hour, so it cannot show that every hour of Tuesday was warmer.
s: (b) No, the report gives only the maximum and minimum, not each hour

questions.q:
Maximum air temperatures over five days: Town A: 34 °C, 33 °C, 33 °C, 32 °C, 31 °C. Town B: 25 °C, 26 °C, 27 °C, 27 °C, 28 °C. Arif claims, 'Town A must be the one heading towards summer, because its temperatures are higher.'
(a) Find the change in Town A's maximum from Day 1 to Day 5.
(b) Find the change in Town B's maximum from Day 1 to Day 5.
(c) Check Arif's claim.
questions.a: (a) It fell by 34 °C - 31 °C = 3 °C. (b) It rose by 28 °C - 25 °C = 3 °C. (c) The claim is wrong: what shows the season is the trend, not how high the values are. Town A's temperature is generally falling, which happens as winter approaches, while Town B's is generally rising, which happens as summer approaches.
s: (c) Claim wrong: the trend matters; A falling (towards winter), B rising (towards summer)

questions.q:
Sameer recorded the weather report for Ranchi for eight successive days in March.
Maximum air temperature (°C): 29, 30, 30, 31, 33, 32, 34, 35
Minimum air temperature (°C): 15, 16, 14, 17, 18, 19, 19, 20
(a) Find the average maximum for the first four days and for the last four days.
(b) On which day was the gap between the maximum and the minimum the largest? Give the gap.
(c) On which day did the maximum fall compared with the day before?
(d) Sameer's friend says that fall shows summer is not approaching. Evaluate this.
(e) If the trend continues, is next week's maximum more likely to be around 28 °C or around 36 °C? Give a reason.
questions.a: (a) First four days: (29 + 30 + 30 + 31) / 4 = 30.0 °C; last four days: (33 + 32 + 34 + 35) / 4 = 33.5 °C. (b) Day 3: 30 °C - 14 °C = 16 °C (the other gaps are 13 °C to 15 °C). (c) Day 6 (33 °C to 32 °C). (d) The friend is wrong: air temperature varies every day because weather depends on several factors, but the overall trend (average up from 30.0 °C to 33.5 °C, minimum up from 15 °C to 20 °C) is rising, as happens when summer approaches. (e) Around 36 °C, since the maximum has been generally rising and was already 35 °C on Day 8.
s: (d) Friend wrong: daily variation, but the overall trend is rising

questions.q:
A school in Kanpur must hold a Class 6 exam in May in whichever of two classrooms is cooler in the afternoon. A room thermometer is hung in each room and read at 2 pm for four days. Room 1: 31 °C, 32 °C, 31 °C, 33 °C. Room 2: 30 °C, 33 °C, 32 °C, 34 °C. The principal remembers that room thermometers give only an approximate idea of room temperature.
(a) Which room was cooler on Day 1?
(b) On how many of the four days was Room 1 the cooler room?
(c) Find the average 2 pm reading for each room.
(d) Which room should the school choose? Justify using (a), (b) and (c).
questions.a: (a) Room 2 (30 °C against 31 °C). (b) Three days (Days 2, 3 and 4). (c) Room 1: (31 + 32 + 31 + 33) / 4 = 31.75 °C; Room 2: (30 + 33 + 32 + 34) / 4 = 32.25 °C. (d) Room 1: although Room 2 was cooler on Day 1, Room 1 was cooler on three of the four days and its average is 0.5 °C lower. Since the readings are only approximate and the difference is small, the choice rests on Room 1 being cooler more often, not on one day's reading.
s: (d) Room 1, using both the count of days and the averages, noting Day 1 went the other way
